name: vde
why: A virtual Ethernet switch that lets you wire up virtual networks and tunnels, a playful way into how Ethernet frames actually move.

brief.what_it_is: VDE (Virtual Distributed Ethernet) is a software Ethernet switch plus virtual cables for building Ethernet networks out of processes and machines. Its vde_switch daemon listens on a UNIX control socket, and vde_plug attaches a process's stdin and stdout to a switch, so frames move between attached units as they would on a real Ethernet segment. A host's tap interface can be bridged onto a switch, and two switches can be joined locally or across machines over ssh or netcat. The output is a virtual LAN that UML machines, the host, or other switches can share. The brew description calls it a virtual Ethernet switch for wiring up virtual networks and tunnels.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames VDE as a way to connect many virtual machines and real hosts into one Ethernet-like network, including across several physical computers and through masqueraded networks. It was based on uml-router and is aimed at User-Mode Linux setups, and it supports mobility, where cables can be swapped without breaking existing connections.
brief.how_it_works: vde_switch is a daemon with a control socket (default /tmp/vde.ctl) that forwards Ethernet frames between plugged-in ports, and it can also run as a hub with -hub. A vde_plug process connects its standard input and output to a switch, and a VDE cable is two plugs joined by a pipe. dpipe, bundled with VDE, is a double pipe that feeds each command's stdout into the other's stdin, which is how a local or ssh-carried cable is built.

commands_seen.context: Synopsis for creating a switch. -unix sets the control socket (default /tmp/vde.ctl), -tap attaches a tap device, -hub makes it broadcast, and -daemon runs it in the background.
Setup step 1 as root: starts a daemon bridged to tap0 in the background.
Gives the tap0 host side an address on the virtual subnet.
Setup step 2, run without root: starts a second switch on a custom control socket.
Joins the default switch and the /tmp/my.ctl switch into one local cable.
Joins a local switch to a switch on a remote machine by running vde_plug on the far end over ssh.
Synopsis for vde_plug. -p picks a switch port, and socketname is the switch's control socket.
Synopsis for dpipe, a double pipe that connects each command's stdout to the other's stdin, since shells do not provide this.
Optional host NAT rule so the virtual network can reach the Internet through eth0.
Mobility step 5: builds a tunnel cable in group 1 bound to a specific source address. A second cable in the same group can then be added and the first removed.

brief.install_notes: The README shows no brew-specific steps. Creating a tap-backed switch needs root, because /dev/net/tun should not be writable by ordinary users. The host needs ifconfig or iproute2 for addressing, and policy routing (ip rule, ip route, rt_tables) for the tunnel example. Remote cables need ssh or netcat on both ends. Routing to the Internet uses ip_forward and iptables, and IPv6 uses radvd with a configured prefix. The README says vde_switch must be compiled with the FSTP flag to enable the spanning-tree work, but it does not describe the build itself.
brief.standout: The transport is just stdin and stdout, so a cable can be any pipe, including ssh, and the dpipe helper is built in because shells do not offer that. Mobility is handled by letting several cables share a group number, so you can move a live network between paths, such as from eth0 to ppp0, without restarting the connections on top.
brief.status: unknown. The fetched README shows copyright lines through 2011 and no release date, last-commit date, or changelog. It is also written in an older style (ifconfig, /proc paths, UML and MPS references) and mentions unfinished FSTP work. I could not confirm current activity from the README alone.
brief.caveats: The README says VDE does not implement spanning tree yet, so a loop in the topology can corrupt MAC forwarding tables and saturate the network. FSTP is described as incomplete and untested against 802.1d/w/s. VLAN 802.1q is described as only almost compatible. Tap mode needs root, and the README warns against making /dev/net/tun writable. Using netcat instead of ssh is explicitly described as insecure. During a cable handoff, multiple cables in one group produce duplicated packets, which can slow traffic. The README notes VDE is not related to www.vde.com. No license is stated in the fetched text. Some README examples use ifconfig and older paths, and the text has typos, such as hich-ups and becouse.
quotes: All units connected to the VDE see each other as they were on a real ethernet.
dpipe cmd1 [arg1] = cmd2 [arg2] it is the double pipe command (it is here just becouse it is not provided by shells).
Please note also that the vde-switches do not manage (yet) the minimum spanning tree protocol thus a loop in the topology can lead to inconsistent MAC forward tables and to network saturation.
fetch_log: https://github.com/virtualsquare/vde-2 : fetched OK, README text returned. No other pages followed because the README is substantive and gives its own usage examples. The README mentions a qemu-vde-HOWTO by Jim Brown, but gives no URL, so it was not fetched.

judge.reason: VDE turns ordinary pipes and SSH connections into virtual Ethernet cables, making network frames and live topology changes something you can explore directly.

entry.title: vde
entry.tldr: A software Ethernet switch you can plug processes, VMs and ssh tunnels into, so you can build and rewire a virtual LAN from the shell.
entry.deeper_look:
VDE, Virtual Distributed Ethernet, is a software Ethernet switch plus virtual cables. The `vde_switch` daemon listens on a UNIX control socket (default `/tmp/vde.ctl`) and forwards Ethernet frames between whatever is plugged into it. It can also run as a hub with `-hub`. The README puts the effect plainly: "All units connected to the VDE see each other as they were on a real ethernet."

The cable is the interesting part. `vde_plug` attaches a process's stdin and stdout to a switch, and a VDE cable is two plugs joined by a pipe. Shells have no way to wire two commands to each other in both directions, so VDE ships `dpipe`, a double pipe that feeds each command's stdout into the other's stdin. Swap one plug for `ssh remote_machine vde_plug` and the cable now runs across the network to a switch on another machine.

VDE was based on uml-router and was aimed at User-Mode Linux setups. The goal is to join many virtual machines and real hosts into one Ethernet-like network, even across several physical computers. A host tap interface can be bridged onto a switch, so the real machine joins the virtual LAN too.

There is also a mobility feature. Several cables can share a group number, so you can add a new path, drop the old one, and move a live network from eth0 to ppp0 without breaking the connections running over it. Along the way you learn how switches learn MACs, what a hub does differently, and why loops are dangerous.
entry.install:
brew install vde
# A tap-backed switch needs root. Remote cables need ssh or netcat on both ends. Host addressing needs ifconfig or iproute2.

try_this.what_happens: Starts a second switch on a custom control socket, without root.
Joins the default switch and the /tmp/my.ctl switch into one local cable.
Joins your local switch to a switch on a remote machine, with ssh carrying the cable.

entry.whats_unique: The cable is just stdin and stdout, so any pipe, including ssh, can be an Ethernet cable. The bundled `dpipe` exists because shells cannot do two-way pipes.
entry.caveats: The README's copyright lines stop at 2011 and it shows no recent activity. It says spanning tree is not implemented, so a loop in your topology can corrupt forwarding tables and saturate the network.
